Let’s evaluate each option step by step.  

**(A) Ammonia is produced in repeated high intensity exercise.**  
True — during intense exercise, ammonia is generated mainly from the deamination of AMP to IMP in muscle, especially when ATP demand is high and phosphocreatine stores are low. This occurs notably in repeated high-intensity efforts.  

**(B) Muscle lactate accumulation does not begin until at least 5 seconds of intermittent muscle contractions have taken place.**  
This seems suspicious. Lactate production can begin very quickly (within the first few seconds) if glycolysis is activated and the rate of pyruvate formation exceeds the mitochondria’s capacity, even before 5 seconds in some cases. However, in very short bursts (<5 s), the primary energy source is ATP and phosphocreatine, and significant lactate accumulation may not be measurable immediately, but “does not begin until at least 5 seconds” is too absolute — some lactate formation can be detected earlier. This statement is likely false because it sets a rigid minimum time threshold not supported by evidence.  

**(C) Muscle phosphocreatine depletion begins in the first few seconds of high intensity exercise.**  
True — phosphocreatine breakdown starts immediately to resynthesize ATP during short, high-intensity efforts.  

**(D) With an increasing number of repeated sprints the rate of accumulation of lactate in muscle declines.**  
True — in repeated sprint protocols, the rate of lactate accumulation per sprint often decreases in later sprints because total lactate production may drop due to fatigue, reduced power output, and greater reliance on aerobic metabolism.  

Thus, the false statement is **(B)**.  

Final answer: (B)
